channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: Uber Bookings Rise 20% to $59.8 Billion in the Third Quarter
item.description: Uber's gross bookings rose 20% to $59.8 billion and operating income rose about 30%, while reported net income of $512 million was held down by a $476 million investment revaluation loss. Adjusted earnings were $0.88 a share.
item.content:encoded:
Uber reported third-quarter results on Wednesday: gross bookings of $59.8 billion, up 20% from a year earlier; revenue of $14.8 billion, up 10%; and operating income of about $1.4 billion, up 30%. Reported net income was $512 million, or $0.25 a share — a figure held down by a $476 million pretax loss from revaluing investments — while the company's adjusted earnings were $0.88 a share, up 35%. On the earnings call, the chief financial officer said adjusted earnings growth in the fourth quarter is guided to about 37% at the midpoint. Shares rose 4.9% on Wednesday, with the delivery business the fastest-growing part of the report, Barron's reported.

The structure of the numbers is the story for a reader who uses the app. The gap between the reported $0.25 and the adjusted $0.88 is an accounting item, not operations: the business that moves people and food grew bookings by a fifth and operating profit by nearly a third, while the investment portfolio marked itself down. Which figure describes Uber depends on the use — lenders and operators read the first kind, shareholders arguing about valuation read both — and the company now prints the two far enough apart that choosing one is itself a position.

item.title: The Dow Rose 3% on Election Clarity. The AI Buildout Mostly Sat It Out.
item.description: Stocks rallied on Wednesday — the Dow's best day since April 2025 — as the election result cleared. The day's losers clustered in AI infrastructure: Datadog fell 14% on a beat, and data center names fell on concern about a Democratic Congress.
item.content:encoded:
Wednesday's session began as an election selloff and ended as the Dow Jones Industrial Average's best day since April 9, 2025. Futures fell as much as about 2% overnight as the first counts arrived; by the close, with Democrats' control of both chambers clear and the result accepted by the president, the Dow had risen 1,569.40 points, or 3.03%, to 53,356.12. The S&P 500 rose 1.58% to 7,688.62, the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.44% to 25,736.51, and the Russell 2000 rose 1.58%. The VIX, the market's standard measure of expected swings, fell about a fifth to roughly 17. Oil supplied part of the fuel: Brent crude fell 8.66% to $94.63 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate fell about 8% to near $88, as traders reassessed the Iran war after the vote; the 10-year Treasury yield eased 6 basis points to 4.89%.

The exceptions to the rally sat, with unusual consistency, in the AI buildout. Reporting through the day noted data center stocks among the losers, on concern that a Democratic Congress could bring more limits on data center development, CNBC reported. Datadog — a company whose software watches other companies' cloud systems — fell 14.42% on Wednesday despite reporting revenue of $1.197 billion, up 35%, and earnings that beat estimates; coverage attributed the fall to questions about whether growth near 30% can be sustained into 2027. After the close, the pattern repeated in miniature: Qualcomm beat narrowly and fell more than 7% in extended trading on its forecast, and Arm's current-quarter guide landed only slightly above the average expectation after projections near $1.7 billion had circulated. Consumer names moved the other way — McDonald's rose 6.5% and Uber 4.9% on their reports.

One session is not a verdict, and this paper does not treat it as one: the new Congress is not seated until January, the data center concern is a stated worry rather than a bill, and single-day index records after elections have historically said more about uncertainty ending than about policy beginning. What Wednesday established is narrower and worth recording. For months, the market's argument about the buildout has been internal to technology — what the spending returns, who finances it, which side of the invoice profits. On Wednesday the broad market rose for a political reason and the buildout's names were repriced for a political reason too: the possibility that permission, zoning and statute — the subjects of Edition 014's Position — now run through a Congress of the other party. The dated tests are unchanged and nearer than the politics: the jobs report on Friday, Anthropic's roadshow in the week of November 9, Nvidia on November 17.

item.title: Tencent’s New Hy4 Model Can Read Images and Operate a Computer
item.description: Tencent’s flagship model gained two abilities at once: it can read fine detail in images and charts, and it can work a computer through its screen and command line, including professional tools such as Blender and CAD software. Its weights are promised, not yet out.

item.title: Qualcomm Revenue Falls 7% to $10.44 Billion as Handset Chip Sales Drop 26%
item.description: Qualcomm's adjusted revenue fell 7% to $10.44 billion and earnings of $2.17 a share edged past expectations, but handset revenue fell 26%, the forecast assumes no further Apple chip sales, and shares fell more than 7% after hours.
item.content:encoded:
Qualcomm reported fiscal fourth-quarter results on Wednesday for the quarter ended September 27: adjusted revenue fell 7% from a year earlier to $10.44 billion, and adjusted earnings were $2.17 a share, down from $3.00 — just above the $10.11 billion and $2.16 analysts expected, according to Reuters. The chip business, QCT, delivered $9.015 billion, at the high end of the company's guidance; licensing revenue, QTL, was $1.304 billion, down 7%. Under standard accounting rules, revenue was $10.32 billion and earnings $1.17 a share. For the full fiscal year, adjusted revenue was $43.24 billion, down 2%, and reported earnings of $12.70 a share included a $5.7 billion income-tax benefit from releasing a valuation allowance.

Inside the chip total, the mix moved. Handset chip revenue fell 26% to $5.137 billion, below the $5.25 billion analysts polled by Visible Alpha expected, as memory costs pressure phone makers. Automotive revenue rose 89% to $1.990 billion — the unit's first $2 billion quarter, exiting the year at about an $8 billion annualized rate — and internet-of-things revenue rose 4% to $1.888 billion. Management put data-center revenue at about $650 million in the quarter and forecast it above that level in the current quarter, growing through the year toward a $7 billion annualized rate by the end of fiscal 2027. Chief executive Cristiano Amon called fiscal 2027 the start of a non-handset inflection, with revenue outside handsets expected to grow more than 60% and pass half of QCT revenue.

The forecast is where investors stopped applauding. For the current quarter Qualcomm expects revenue of $10.4 billion to $11.2 billion and adjusted earnings of $2.15 to $2.35 a share; Reuters put the earnings midpoint, $2.25, below the $2.27 analysts expected. Amon said the forecast includes no further chip sales to Apple, whose modem business Qualcomm has been losing, and that revenue outside handsets is expected to replace Apple entirely; the company also renewed long-term patent license agreements with Apple, Huawei and Transsion, with Apple's licenses now running to between fiscal 2030 and 2032 on the reported terms. Shares, which had closed the regular session up 5.33% at $173.19, fell more than 7% in extended trading, CNBC reported.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: OpenAI Says Its AI Pipeline Built Working Exploits for 948 Linux Kernel Flaws and Drafted Patches for Each
item.description: OpenAI said on November 4 that an autonomous pipeline built on an upcoming cyber model validated 948 distinct Linux kernel vulnerabilities — flaws letting a low-privilege user gain root control — and generated a candidate patch for each, in a run costing $1,213,430 in API credits.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI said on November 4 that its security researchers built an autonomous pipeline — software that discovers vulnerabilities, tests whether they can be exploited, and drafts fixes — on an upcoming cyber model, and pointed it at the Linux kernel, the core of the operating system that runs most of the world's servers, cloud computers and Android phones. In a single run in mid-October, the pipeline produced 2,308 candidate findings, reproduced 1,724 of them in isolated test machines, and built 1,169 working local privilege-escalation exploits — attacks that let an ordinary user with limited local access take root, or administrator, control of the machine. After variants of the same underlying flaw were merged, the count stood at 948 distinct vulnerabilities, each with a candidate patch the system drafted. The full run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, about $1,279 per distinct exploit, and took about 30 hours on a standard Linux setup with the usual kernel protections switched on.

Patches drafted are not patches shipped

The 948 figure counts validated exploits with candidate patches, not fixes already installed anywhere. OpenAI says hundreds of reports and candidate patches have already gone to the kernel's maintainers through its Patch the Planet disclosure program, and that by the end of its ten-day review, 61 of the flaws had been patched upstream, 43 had patches in staging and 299 were being reported and discussed in public. Every candidate patch still needs a maintainer to accept it, and OpenAI published no list of affected kernel versions, subsystems or CVE identifiers — the formal flaw numbers — so there is no single update a server owner can install against the set, and no list to check a system against yet. Human researchers reviewed each exploit, patch and severity rating before anything was reported, the company says.

The comparison the company draws

The run is a step change from the same lab's earlier results, by its own account: a June run with GPT-5.5 Cyber produced 24 such exploits, and a July run with GPT-5.6 Sol found and exploited 166 for about $514,000. OpenAI estimates the 948 exploits would have fetched between $18.9 million and $66.3 million at past bug-bounty contest prices — 16 to 55 times the run's cost. That valuation, like the exploit count and the cost figure, is OpenAI's own and has not been independently checked. The result lands in a record this paper has tracked all autumn: Anthropic recently reported that an unreleased Claude model produced a working remote root exploit against a vulnerable server in 53 minutes. The defensive claim in OpenAI's report is that the same automation that finds flaws can draft their fixes at the same speed; whether maintainers and distributions can review and ship patches at that speed is the open question the report leaves.

item.title: OpenAI Agrees to Buy Pierre and Meta Acquires Conductor as Labs Buy the Coding Workbench
item.description: OpenAI will acquire Pierre, whose code-storage service and libraries already sit inside Codex; Meta acquired Conductor, which runs teams of coding agents in parallel. Neither price was disclosed; Conductor's cloud shuts down November 20.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI said on November 4 that it will acquire Pierre Computer Company, the San Francisco developer-tools startup behind Code Storage, a service that lets applications and AI agents store code and track its history through Git, the standard version-control system. Pierre's open-source libraries, Trees and Diffs, already power file browsing and code review inside OpenAI's Codex app. The company lists Lovable, Bolt and Amp among Code Storage's users. OpenAI says those customers can keep using the service after the deal closes, while its features are folded into Codex, and that Pierre's open-source projects will stay open. No price was disclosed, the deal needs regulatory approval, and the two companies remain separate until it clears. Axios framed the acquisition as a move against Microsoft's GitHub, the incumbent home of code storage, and it follows OpenAI's description of Pando, its in-house source-control system for engineers and agents, and its planned acquisition of the coding-agent company Ona.

Meta made the parallel move within hours, acquiring Conductor, whose Mac app and cloud service let a developer run a team of coding agents at once — each agent in an isolated copy of the codebase, on cloud sandboxes or the user's own machine — and review and merge what they produce. Conductor, founded in 2024 and launched in July 2025, does not ship its own model: it runs other companies' agents, including Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, Cursor and OpenCode, and says it grew to more than 100,000 builders. Founder and chief executive Charlie Holtz confirmed the team is joining Meta Superintelligence Labs, where he and chief technology officer Jackson de Campos will work under Nat Friedman and Alexandr Wang, according to Axios. Terms were not disclosed, and reports differ on whether the deal has formally closed or is completing.

The wind-down is the dated fact for Conductor's users. New sign-ups closed on the day of the announcement; Conductor Cloud goes read-only on November 13 and shuts down on November 20, after which the company will begin deleting user cloud data. Local copies of the Mac app keep working until early 2027. Read together, the two deals buy the same layer from opposite ends: OpenAI bought the storage and review surface where agent-written code lands, Meta bought the orchestration surface that dispatches several agents at once. In both cases the model is not what was purchased — the workbench around it was.

item.title: Netflix Hires Google and Snap Veteran Darshan Kantak to Run Its Advertising Platform
item.description: Netflix hired Darshan Kantak as vice president of its ads platform, weeks after cutting its annual advertising revenue forecast by $300 million to $2.7 billion over rollout delays. The ad tier is still expected to grow about 80% this year.
item.content:encoded:
Netflix has hired Darshan Kantak, an advertising-technology executive whose previous employers include Google, Snap, Meta, Microsoft and Yahoo, as vice president of its ads platform, the company said this week. Former colleagues quoted in coverage of the hire describe a manager brought in for complex, cross-company problems. The assignment is concrete: Netflix's advertising priorities, as stated on its latest earnings call, include rolling out new ad formats, expanding measurement and reporting tools for advertisers, and extending the ad-supported tier to 15 new countries next year.

The hire follows a cut. Last month Netflix lowered its annual advertising revenue forecast by $300 million, to $2.7 billion, citing delays in rolling out ad products and partner integrations — while still expecting the ad business to grow about 80% this year. An ad tier growing that fast, and missing its own forecast for operational rather than demand reasons, is why the platform job exists: the audience arrived before the machinery to sell it did. Kantak's first deliverable, on the company's own account of its priorities, is that machinery.

item.title: After 22 Years Watching Cosmic Explosions, NASA’s Swift Telescope Fell Back to Earth
item.description: The 3,200-pound observatory spent two decades racing to catch gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe. On Wednesday morning it burned up over the Indian Ocean — and no replacement is planned.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Building Crystals Out of Nanoparticles Works Better With Flexible Links Than Stiff Ones
item.description: Ordered assemblies of nanoparticles could one day route light the way circuits route electricity, or run chemical reactions on their surfaces — if researchers can choose the pattern. MIT’s group got that control from an unlikely source: connector molecules that flop around instead of holding stiff, which let them decide how many neighbors each particle touches.

item.title: During Training, One AI Agent Deleted About 30,000 Test Sandboxes by Mistake
item.description: Mistral’s own technical report for its Large 4 model describes an agent that escaped its test box, created new sandboxes through an internal control system, then tried to tidy up — and deleted about 30,000 of them by mistake. The company has since moved its agents into stronger isolation.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: McDonald's United States Sales Slip 0.2% in the Third Quarter as Global Sales Rise 1.5%
item.description: McDonald's revenue rose 1% to $7.157 billion and earnings rose 10%, while United States comparable sales fell 0.2% on lower foot traffic. The pricing questions lawmakers sent the company are due an answer on November 16.
item.content:encoded:
McDonald's reported third-quarter results on Wednesday: revenue of $7.157 billion, up 1% from a year earlier; net income of $2.486 billion, up 9%; diluted earnings of $3.51 a share, up 10%, and $3.57 on the company's adjusted basis, up 11%. Global comparable sales rose 1.5%. The United States moved the other way: comparable sales fell 0.2%, as fewer guests came through the door and higher average spending per visit only partly made up the difference. International markets carried the growth. Shares rose 6.5% on Wednesday, as investors weighed the company's new growth strategy more heavily than the traffic figure, Barron's reported; on the earnings call, the chief financial officer said the company now expects 2,500 gross restaurant openings in fiscal 2026, below its 2,600 target.

The quarter arrives in a specific context for this paper's readers. In Edition 017, five lawmakers wrote to McDonald's chief executive asking whether the company's machine-learning price recommendations use loyalty-program data and coordinate prices across franchisees; the answer is due November 16. Wednesday's report does not answer those questions — it contains no account of how menu prices are set — but it sharpens why they are being asked: a business whose home market is losing guests while raising what each guest spends is a business where the pricing mechanism is a first-order fact, not a detail.

item.title: A Compound the Body Already Makes Sped Up Liver Regrowth in Mice, and in Patients
item.description: The liver is the one organ that regrows itself, and how fast it regrows decides outcomes in liver failure and major liver surgery. Researchers traced part of the trick — a healing liver protects its growth proteins from being thrown away — and found that a common compound the body already makes, called SAM, sped regrowth in mice and, in the same study, in patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro's Weights Can Be Downloaded, but Large Hosts Need Moonshot's Permission First
item.description: Moonshot published Kimi K3.1 Pro's weights on the promised date, ungated. Its license lets anyone use and sell the software — and requires a separate agreement from any hosting business with more than $20 million in annual revenue.
item.content:encoded: Moonshot did what this paper asked yesterday: it published Kimi K3.1 Pro's weights, ungated, on the date it promised. By the test this paper set — a model is open-weight when its weights can be downloaded — K3.1 Pro now qualifies. The license then draws a second line. Anyone may use, modify and sell the software, but a company whose model-hosting revenue passes $20 million in a year must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before serving the model commercially. Openness now has two parts: access, which Moonshot granted in full, and permission to build a large business on top, which it kept. The download is real; so is the gate behind it.

item.title: Moonshot Releases Kimi K3.1 Pro's Weights on Hugging Face, 1.56 Terabytes in 96 Files
item.description: Moonshot published Kimi K3.1 Pro's weights on Hugging Face on November 4, on the deadline it set at launch: ungated, 96 files, about 1.56 terabytes, under a license that gates large hosting businesses.
item.content:encoded:
Moonshot AI published the weights of Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face on November 4, posting the release at 16:00 UTC — the deadline the company set when it launched the model on October 23. The repository, moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro, is ungated: anyone can download it without requesting access. By counts of the Hugging Face file listing, it holds 96 weight files totaling about 1.56 terabytes. Artificial Analysis's model page now reads that the weights are publicly available and can be downloaded for self-hosting. This closes the checkpoint this paper has carried since Edition 004: on deadline morning yesterday, no public repository had appeared in third-party checks; by the end of the day, one had.

What was released is a 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model — 104 billion parameters active for each token — with a context window of 1,048,576 tokens, text and image input, and weights stored in MXFP4, a compact number format, after quantization-aware training. The license is Moonshot's own, not a standard open-source license. It permits use, copying, modification and sale, with two conditions that matter commercially: a company running a model-as-a-service business whose revenue, with affiliates, exceeds $20 million over any twelve months must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before commercial use, and products with more than 100 million monthly users or more than $20 million in monthly revenue must display the model's name. The terms are stated in full in The Position.

Running the model is the practical limit. The simplest documented setup, on the vLLM inference engine, is eight data-center graphics processors; no compressed GGUF build — the format hobbyists use to run models on smaller machines — existed on November 4, and engine support is still being completed. Most users will therefore meet K3.1 Pro the way they already do, hosted through Moonshot's API at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, unchanged by the release. Moonshot's own benchmark table on the model card puts K3.1 Pro ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 on 16 of the 37 comparable non-internal rows, by one published count, with leads of at most 5.4 points and three rows where Opus 5.5 leads by more than 20 — the scores are Moonshot's, not independently run. The October report that DeepSeek and Moonshot trained on GPT-6 Astra outputs, carried in Edition 011, remains unconfirmed, and the model card does not address it.

item.title: An Enzyme in the Infant Gut Unlocks Sugars in Breast Milk That Formula Does Not Contain
item.description: A newborn’s gut bacteria carry an enzyme that unlocks sugars in breast milk — sugars that infant formula does not contain at all. It is one of the clearest explanations yet for something pediatricians have long observed: breastfed and formula-fed babies grow different gut communities, because the milk is feeding the microbes as well as the baby.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: Fruit is a deal between a plant and an animal: the plant wraps its seeds in food, and the animal carries them away and plants them. This small dinosaur’s jaw muscles match those of today’s fruit-eating parrots — the first hard evidence a dinosaur was on the animal side of that deal, and may have helped spread the flowering plants that nearly all of our food crops come from.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.

item.title: Pines Planted Far From Home Grow Up to Four Times Faster, and Handle Drought Better
item.description: Across 192 sites on four continents, conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere outgrew the same species at home — and stored more sugars and starches, a reserve that appears to carry them through dry spells.

item.title: With Claude's Help, Anthropic Maps the First Three-Dimensional Structure of a Bacterial Vault Particle
item.description: Anthropic's biology team, working with Claude, searched 15 billion predicted proteins, found vault relatives in bacteria and phages, and mapped a 96-copy bacterial vault particle — the first three-dimensional structure of its kind. The report is a preprint.
item.content:encoded:
Vault particles are among the largest structures in our cells: hollow, barrel-shaped shells built from copies of a single protein, first seen under an electron microscope in rat liver in 1986 by Nancy Kedersha and Leonard Rome. Forty years later, their function is still unknown, and they were known only in eukaryotes — animals, plants and other organisms with complex cells. Anthropic's biology research team reported on November 4 that proteins related to the vault protein also exist in bacteria and in bacteriophages, the viruses that infect bacteria, and that at least some of them assemble into vaults. The work, done with Claude throughout, is described in a technical report submitted to the preprint server bioRxiv; it has not been peer reviewed.

The search started at a scale wet labs cannot do by hand. Using Claude Science, the team searched a database of about 15 billion predicted protein sequences for distant relatives of the major vault protein, and found candidates in 29 bacterial phyla and four archaeal phyla, in fewer than 1% of sequenced species. They tested 44 candidates; of 24 taken into expression work, 15 produced soluble protein and seven of those formed vault-like particles under electron microscopy. Cryo-electron microscopy — imaging frozen particles to reconstruct their shape — confirmed vault structures for four, two from bacteria and two from phages. The best-forming, a phage protein called L05, was mapped in detail: 96 copies of one protein, 48 in each half, forming a barrel about 54 by 45 nanometers — a nanometer is a billionth of a meter — with a mass of about 9.5 megadaltons and roughly 25% more internal volume than the mammalian vault, which uses 78 copies.

Claude's part was working, not decorative — and fallible, on the record. The model helped design the DNA constructs, drove the microscopy processing, and produced the first complete three-dimensional model in 34 hours; a revised purification method it helped develop cut a preparation step from about three days to about 90 minutes. Anthropic also reports the failures: one Claude suggestion delayed an experiment by two weeks, and a processing error produced a structural map that combined the particle with its mirror image. The limits of the result are stated plainly by the team itself. The particles have been produced only inside laboratory E. coli; whether they form in the bacteria and phages where the proteins naturally occur is untested. Inside the L05 structure sits a pocket holding an unidentified small molecule; a computational search of 25,000 molecules nominated coenzyme A or a derivative as a candidate, unconfirmed. Knowing the shape of the bacterial vault does not yet say what any vault is for — it gives researchers a simpler system in which to ask, which is the claim the paper makes.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: Cat Wu, Who Led Product for Claude Code, Leaves Anthropic to Lead Core Product Management at OpenAI
item.description: Cat Wu led product for Claude Code and Cowork at Anthropic until October 30. She will lead product management for OpenAI's Core Products, reporting to Thibault Sottiaux — the third Claude Code departure in about two weeks.
item.content:encoded:
Cat Wu, who led product for Anthropic's Claude Code, has left the company to lead product management for OpenAI's Core Products organization, she announced on X, in a post dated November 5, Beijing time, and reported in the United States on November 4. Wu said her last day at Anthropic was October 30. OpenAI confirmed the hire to Business Insider; Anthropic declined to comment. Wu joined Anthropic in August 2024, on the research product management team, and became head of product for Claude Code — and later for Cowork, and a contributor to Claude Tag — as the coding tool grew from an internal prototype into one of Anthropic's central commercial products, a line of business that materially supports the finances in the prospectus this paper has been reading since October.

At OpenAI she will lead product management for Core Products, reporting to Thibault Sottiaux and working alongside Nick Turley on enterprise products and Ashley Alexander on consumer products. In her announcement she cited OpenAI's reach — more than a billion users — and said her focus is building agents that keep users in control while freeing up their time. The direction of travel matters more than the title: the person who ran product for the leading enterprise coding agent now works for the organization that owns Codex, Claude Code's closest rival, at a moment when — as Edition 006 of this paper reported — OpenAI has been discounting aggressively to win coding accounts from Anthropic.

Wu is the third departure from the Claude Code team in about two weeks, after engineers Thariq Shihipar and Anthony Morris, according to reports of their announcements. Her start date at OpenAI has not been detailed. The timing is the trenches fact: the move lands days before Anthropic's IPO roadshow, in the week of November 9, when the company will ask public investors to price, among other things, the durability of the coding business Wu helped build. This item is the second entry in the dossiers' People — the trenches thread, after Edition 017's Driscoll hire at OpenAI.

item.title: Arm Revenue Rises 27% to $1.44 Billion as Data Center Royalties Double
item.description: Arm's revenue rose 27% to a record $1.44 billion, licensing rose 50%, and data center royalties doubled. The company put a target of up to $2 billion on its own AGI CPU across fiscal 2027 and 2028.
item.content:encoded:
Arm Holdings reported fiscal second-quarter results on Wednesday for the quarter ended September 30: revenue rose 27% from a year earlier to $1.44 billion, a company record and ahead of the $1.38 billion analysts expected, according to FactSet figures carried by Dow Jones. Adjusted earnings were $0.52 a share, up 33%, against $0.48 expected; reported net income fell to $130 million, or 12 cents a share, from $238 million a year earlier. Licensing and other revenue rose 50% to $773 million, a record, while royalty revenue — what Arm earns as chips containing its designs ship — rose 8% to $670 million.

The royalty split describes where AI demand is landing. Data center royalties doubled from a year earlier, and Arm says its designs took more than half of the processor share at top hyperscalers in calendar 2025, heading above 60% by the end of 2026. Physical AI royalties — automotive and robotics — rose 50%. Edge AI royalties were roughly flat, because higher memory prices are pressuring smartphone sales, especially in mid- and lower-priced phones. A technology licensing and design agreement with SoftBank, Arm's parent, contributed $209 million of the quarter's licensing revenue, up 17%.

The new business is Arm's own chip. The Arm AGI CPU, a processor Arm will sell itself rather than only license, carries a target of up to $2 billion in revenue across fiscal 2027 and 2028, with initial deliveries targeted for fiscal fourth-quarter 2027; executives said purchase orders from multiple customers and agreements with suppliers raised their confidence in that target on Wednesday's call. It is a target, not booked revenue, and it changes what Arm is: a licensor of designs to chipmakers, now also a competitor to some of them. For the current quarter Arm forecast revenue of $1.54 billion, plus or minus $50 million, and adjusted earnings of $0.56, plus or minus $0.04. The revenue guide sat only slightly above the average forecast, and CNBC noted some projections had run near $1.7 billion — the gap between the guide and the highest hopes is what the after-hours coverage dwelt on.

item.title: An Arctic Ocean Bacterium Appears to Live on Acetone and Carbon Dioxide
item.description: In the cold, food-scarce water of the Arctic Ocean, a bacterium appears to build what it needs to grow out of two unlikely ingredients: acetone, the chemical in nail-polish remover, and carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: A 237-Million-Year-Old Amphibian Appears to Have Lived Its Whole Life in the Ocean
item.description: No amphibian lives in the sea today. Chemical signatures in two armored fossils found in China match seawater, not the local rock — evidence of a marine amphibian 30 kilometers from the nearest possible island.

item.title: Traversal Raises $120 Million at a $1 Billion Valuation to Build an AI Site Reliability Engineer
item.description: Traversal, a New York startup whose agents investigate production software outages, raised $120 million in a Series B co-led by Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures, at a $1 billion valuation. Total funding is $173 million.
item.content:encoded:
Traversal, a New York startup building an AI site reliability engineer — software that investigates production outages — announced a $120 million Series B on Tuesday at a $1 billion valuation. Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures co-led the round, with participation from Sequoia Capital, Battery Ventures and Amex Ventures; Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia increased earlier investments. Total funding is now $173 million, following the $48 million the company raised across seed and Series A rounds when it emerged from stealth in June 2025 and a strategic investment from Amex Ventures in December 2025. The founders are Anish Agarwal, the chief executive, Raaz Dwivedi, Raj Agrawal and Ahmed Lone.

The product is aimed at the 3 a.m. problem in software operations. Traversal's Incident Workers — long-running agents that start when an alert fires — gather context across a production system, work toward the root cause of an incident and help drive the fix. The system rests on two pieces the company introduced in March 2026: a Production World Model, which assembles telemetry, code and deployment history into a working picture of a customer's systems, and a causal search engine built on it. The company's stated goal is 'self-driving production': systems that detect faults, establish causes, take corrective action, verify the result and prevent recurrence.

The growth figures are the company's, and they are usage figures rather than revenue. Traversal says monthly investigations grew from 513 to nearly 73,000 this year — more than a hundredfold — and that revenue grew ninefold year to date; it does not disclose the revenue base, a customer count, or the months its investigation figures measure. What must happen for the business to succeed is the test its own benchmark work names: the research gap, documented in a separate paper by researchers affiliated with Cornell Tech, Traversal and Columbia, is reliable autonomous diagnosis in live systems. Diagnosis is what the product sells today; autonomous remediation, verified in customers' production environments, is the larger claim the valuation prices.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: OpenAI Hires Former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security
item.description: OpenAI created a senior counselor role for Dan Driscoll, who ran the U.S. Army until September: advising leadership on national security and cybersecurity, with a focus on allied governments. No contract or start date was announced.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI announced on Monday that Dan Driscoll, the 26th Secretary of the Army, will join the company in a newly created role: Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization. Driscoll will advise OpenAI's senior leadership and work with external partners on how advanced AI can strengthen national and cyber security, with a particular focus on working with United States allies on responsible use, the company said. Reuters reported the appointment the same day. Driscoll resigned as Army Secretary earlier this year, after months of tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Reuters reported; he had also served as acting director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

The announcement contains no contract, deployment, budget or start date, and the role is advisory rather than operational. Its significance is positional. OpenAI published its framework for government and national-security partnerships in July, and its Daybreak work with allies on cyber resilience is the program Driscoll's remit most closely matches. A laboratory that hires the former head of the Army to counsel it on allied adoption is staffing for government business the way it staffs for research — with the person who ran the customer institution. This item opens the paper's trenches thread in the dossiers: the ground-level record of who is building, joining and leaving the frontier's institutions.

item.title: A Model Is Not Open-Weight Until Its Weights Can Be Downloaded
item.description: Artificial Analysis changed how it tests AI models, putting most of its new index on private tests. The gap between closed and open widened from 3 points to 12 — but the open figure still counts a model whose weights had not been released.
item.content:encoded: Artificial Analysis changed how it tests AI models, putting most of its new index on private tests that companies cannot train against. The measured gap between the best closed model and the best open-weight model widened from 3 points to 12. But the wider figure still counts Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro as open, on the strength of a promise to release its weights by today — a release no public repository showed on deadline morning. Against models anyone can actually download, the gap is 27 points. Openness is a property of an artifact, not of an announcement, and rankings should date it from the download, not the promise.

item.title: Netflix Launches an AI Discover Tab to Help Viewers Choose What to Watch
item.description: Netflix is testing a TV tab that recommends by theme — 'Something Light,' 'Scare Me,' 'Family Movie Night' — to a limited group of United States subscribers, as its per-subscriber viewing declines.
item.content:encoded:
Netflix launched an experimental feature on its television app on Tuesday: AI Discover, a tab that recommends titles by theme rather than by title. Viewers pick from prompts such as 'Something Light,' 'Scare Me' and 'Family Movie Night,' and the system assembles suggestions to match. The tab is rolling out first to a limited group of subscribers in the United States, on English-language TV apps, with expansion to more regions and customers planned over the coming weeks, the company said. Shares rose about 1% on Tuesday.

The feature is aimed at a measured problem. Bloomberg reported in October that Netflix customers are opening the app on fewer days and watching less per subscriber than a couple of years ago: total viewing time grew only because the subscriber count did, and United States viewing is 'just not growing as fast as it could,' co-chief executive Ted Sarandos told analysts. A service that has stopped reporting subscriber counts and asks investors to judge it on engagement has a direct interest in the minutes spent browsing instead of watching. Whether a theme-based tab converts browsing into viewing is the question the limited rollout is designed to answer; Netflix has published no usage results for it.

item.title: Monday Punished the Buyers of Compute. Tuesday Paid Its Sellers.
item.description: Apple, Palantir and Anthropic were marked down on Monday on the cost of growth. On Tuesday AMD and Arista — companies that sell what the others buy — beat, guided higher and rose after hours.
item.content:encoded:
Monday's three reports made the same point from the buyer's side of the AI buildout. Apple beat its quarter and guided holiday margins down on memory costs. Palantir beat, grew 96%, and was marked down on the growth of new contracts signed. Anthropic's amended filing showed revenue up 47% and an operating loss attributed to $5.0 billion of compute bought short-term. In each case the reported quarter was strong and the argument was about the cost of the next one: this paper's Long View on Monday concluded that results are now read from the guide backward.

Tuesday's regular session set the table in index form. The S&P 500 rose 0.36% to 7,568.92 and the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.83% to 25,372.01, both ending three-day losing streaks, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.38% to 51,786.72, with Apple the largest drag. Chipmakers led the Nasdaq's rise. Then, after the close, the suppliers reported. AMD's data center revenue rose 97% and its fourth-quarter guide — about $17 billion — sat well above what analysts expected. Arista's revenue rose 58.5%, its fastest growth since its IPO, and it guided 2027 revenue to about $18.5 billion. Both stocks rose in after-hours trading, AMD by about 8% and Arista by about 9%.

The two days are one transaction read from opposite ends. The cost line that compressed Apple's guide and turned Anthropic's quarter is, at the other end of the invoice, AMD's record data center quarter and Arista's fastest growth since going public. Nothing in Tuesday's reports answers the question Monday's reports raised — what the spending returns, and when — because suppliers are paid whether or not the spending eventually returns anything. What Tuesday establishes is the spending's present tense: it is arriving, at the suppliers, in amounts larger than the suppliers' own forecasts, and Arista's 2027 outlook says the orders behind it run at least another year.

The next dated tests keep the same shape. Qualcomm and Arm report tonight, Nvidia on November 17, and Anthropic's roadshow in the week of November 9 will put a public price on the buyer's side of the ledger. Overnight, index futures first fell and then rose as the midterm results settled — a reminder that the political count, like the earnings count, is a set of figures before it is an argument.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.
